bull_bear.body:
- scale: one of the largest midstream lighterage fleets in India — evidence: 63 self-propelled barges, 8 mini bulk carriers, 9 floating cranes, 11 tugs and 1 coastal vessel at FY2026 year-end, plus 370+ earthmoving and shore-handling equipment
- integration: owned sea-to-shore logistics loop from lighterage to shore handling and inland transport — evidence: owned barges, floating cranes and tugs plus 370+ shore-handling units; 16.87 MMT cargo handled and 3.09 MMT cargo transported in FY2026
- distribution: multi-port footprint at Gujarat non-major ports — evidence: three-decade operating presence at Navlakhi, Bedi, Magdalla, Bhavnagar and Dharamtar — against it: the company itself lists dependence on key customers and on Gujarat-coast ports as a concentration risk
- customer lock-in: repeat international government-linked contract — evidence: Ceylon Shipping Corporation coal lightering agreement for the Lakvijaya Power Plant, in place since 2021, extended in June 2026 for two further contract years to 31 May 2028 on unchanged terms
- integration: in-house dry-docking and vessel building to cut fleet downtime — evidence: dry dock yard near Bedi Port with State-level clearances received [planned] — against it: Central-level clearances still in process and the yard is in the name of the Promoter, with ownership presently not transferable for regulatory reasons
- integration: mining-to-movement participation in coal, the largest cargo category — evidence: 37% JV Shreeji Nuravi Chuperbhita Simlong Mines has acquired approximately 1,720 hectares, with coal production targeted from May 2027 [planned] — against it: forest and environment clearance applications are still in final stages of submission
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Cargo-volume and vessel-mix risk — Demand for stevedoring, lighterage and handling services depends on dry-bulk cargo volumes at the ports served (linked to commodity demand, import policies and customer dispatch programmes) and on the mix of geared versus gearless vessels calling there, which drives floating-crane and lighterage demand.
- Monsoon seasonality — Operations at seasonal ports are affected by the monsoon, hitting fleet utilisation; mitigation relies on inducting all-weather mini bulk carriers, with the all-weather count to double to 4 by Q3 FY2027.
- Customer and geographic concentration — Dependence on key customers and on Gujarat-coast ports, with customer and sector concentration inherent in a B2B port-services model; mitigation depends on customer additions and the eastern-India and coastal-movement expansion.
- Project and regulatory-clearance risk — The dry dock yard awaits Central-level clearances and the mining JV's schedule depends on forest, environment and consent approvals; delays would defer the associated revenue streams.
- Fuel and crewing cost inflation — Bunker and diesel price volatility and crewing cost inflation affect operating costs; mitigated through contract structures and operating efficiency.
- Foreign exchange risk — Exposure arises from Sri Lanka operations and USD-denominated receivables.
- Regulatory and compliance risk — The group operates within evolving maritime, tax, labour and environmental frameworks, including the newly notified Labour Codes.

business.body: Shreeji Shipping Global is primarily a stevedoring, lighterage and port-handling company for dry-bulk cargo such as coal, pet coke and sulphur, operating an integrated sea-to-shore logistics loop of owned barges, floating cranes, tugs, mini bulk carriers and shore handling / earthmoving equipment. It serves industrial B2B customers at Gujarat non-major ports (Navlakhi, Bedi, Magdalla, Bhavnagar) and Dharamtar, and performs coal lightering and barging for the Lakvijaya Power Plant at Puttalam, Sri Lanka. outlook.body:
- Scale coastal cargo movement as a core business, building on MV SJ Lily (deployed under time charter through the wholly-owned GIFT City IFSC subsidiary) and other coastal vessels, moving from port-based lighterage towards an integrated shipping & logistics company.
- Extend the footprint to India's east coast with floating-crane lighterage operations at Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata.
- Establish a dry dock yard near Bedi Port, Jamnagar, to build new coastal vessels and dry-dock the own fleet in-house (reducing downtime and laid-up periods) and to build and repair vessels for third-party domestic and international shipowners; structure of participation still being evaluated, with any promoter-group arrangements on arm's-length terms.
- Evaluate development, acquisition or construction of one to two jetties in Gujarat and Maharashtra to deepen integration from ship's hold to customer's gate.
- Participate across the coal mining-to-movement chain via the JV Shreeji Nuravi Chuperbhita Simlong Mines Private Limited (Chuperbhita Simlong open-cast coal project).
- Convert a seasonal business into an increasingly all-season one by inducting all-weather vessels with round-the-year plying permission.
- Deploy IPO proceeds with discipline: vessel acquisition only when asset values, charter economics and available vessels meet return thresholds.
- Develop small jetties jointly with coastal industries located away from major ports, deploying own barges, floating cranes and handling equipment for long-duration, relationship-anchored operations.

outlook.body: FY2027 expansion priorities set out by the Chairman: scale the coastal cargo movement business built around MV SJ Lily and other coastal vessels (coastal movement commenced during FY2026 through the IFSC subsidiary as well as with the company's own coastal vessels); commission floating-crane lighterage operations at Kolkata and take delivery of two mini bulk carriers on schedule; advance a dry dock yard through its remaining Central-level clearances; progress evaluation of strategic jetty locations in Gujarat and Maharashtra; support the mining joint venture through its clearance milestones towards first coal; and deploy IPO proceeds for vessel acquisition only when asset values, charter economics and available vessels meet return thresholds, with any change to the objects of the Issue subject to shareholder approval. Project and regulatory-clearance risk is managed through staged capital commitment aligned to approval milestones.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Demand is driven principally by dry-bulk cargo volumes (coal, pet coke, sulphur) at the ports served, whose movement management describes as comparatively resilient across economic cycles.
- The mix of geared versus gearless vessels calling at served ports determines demand for the floating cranes and lighterage fleet.
- Monsoon seasonality at seasonal ports is a key operating sensitivity.
- The company does not operate ocean-going vessels on international routes, so global freight and charter-rate cycles do not affect earnings directly.
- Outlook supported by the importance of non-major and tidal ports, especially Gujarat, the largest non-major port market in India, where the company is established.
- Government emphasis on coastal shipping, port modernisation, multimodal connectivity and private-sector participation is expected to support gradual expansion of cargo volumes and marine logistics activity at these ports.
- Approval of eligible inland vessels under the Tonnage Tax Scheme (Chapter XII-G), effective FY2026, is described as a structural improvement to long-term tax efficiency and cash generation.
- Company enters FY2027 with a materially larger owned fleet, a net-cash balance sheet, tonnage-tax efficiency and an extended international engagement.
- Sri Lanka: agreement with Ceylon Shipping Corporation Limited for coal lightering and barging for the Lakvijaya Power Plant (Puttalam Port), in place since 2021, extended in June 2026 for two further contract years from 1 June 2026 to 31 May 2028 on existing terms.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Shreeji Shipping Global is primarily a stevedoring, lighterage and port-handling company for dry-bulk cargo such as coal, pet coke and sulphur, operating an integrated sea-to-shore logistics loop of owned barges, floating cranes, tugs, mini bulk carriers and shore handling / earthmoving equipment. It serves industrial B2B customers at Gujarat non-major ports (Navlakhi, Bedi, Magdalla, Bhavnagar) and Dharamtar, and performs coal lightering and barging for the Lakvijaya Power Plant at Puttalam, Sri Lanka. It does not operate ocean-going vessels on international routes, and in FY2026 began domestic coastal cargo movement through its wholly-owned GIFT City IFSC subsidiary.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Demand is driven principally by dry-bulk cargo volumes (coal, pet coke, sulphur) at the ports served, whose movement management describes as comparatively resilient across economic cycles.
- The mix of geared versus gearless vessels calling at served ports determines demand for the floating cranes and lighterage fleet.
- Monsoon seasonality at seasonal ports is a key operating sensitivity.
- The company does not operate ocean-going vessels on international routes, so global freight and charter-rate cycles do not affect earnings directly.
- Outlook supported by the importance of non-major and tidal ports, especially Gujarat, the largest non-major port market in India, where the company is established.
- Government emphasis on coastal shipping, port modernisation, multimodal connectivity and private-sector participation is expected to support gradual expansion of cargo volumes and marine logistics activity at these ports.
- Approval of eligible inland vessels under the Tonnage Tax Scheme (Chapter XII-G), effective FY2026, is described as a structural improvement to long-term tax efficiency and cash generation.
- Company enters FY2027 with a materially larger owned fleet, a net-cash balance sheet, tonnage-tax efficiency and an extended international engagement.
- Sri Lanka: agreement with Ceylon Shipping Corporation Limited for coal lightering and barging for the Lakvijaya Power Plant (Puttalam Port), in place since 2021, extended in June 2026 for two further contract years from 1 June 2026 to 31 May 2028 on existing terms.

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Scale coastal cargo movement as a core business, building on MV SJ Lily (deployed under time charter through the wholly-owned GIFT City IFSC subsidiary) and other coastal vessels, moving from port-based lighterage towards an integrated shipping & logistics company.
- Extend the footprint to India's east coast with floating-crane lighterage operations at Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata.
- Establish a dry dock yard near Bedi Port, Jamnagar, to build new coastal vessels and dry-dock the own fleet in-house (reducing downtime and laid-up periods) and to build and repair vessels for third-party domestic and international shipowners; structure of participation still being evaluated, with any promoter-group arrangements on arm's-length terms.
- Evaluate development, acquisition or construction of one to two jetties in Gujarat and Maharashtra to deepen integration from ship's hold to customer's gate.
- Participate across the coal mining-to-movement chain via the JV Shreeji Nuravi Chuperbhita Simlong Mines Private Limited (Chuperbhita Simlong open-cast coal project).
- Convert a seasonal business into an increasingly all-season one by inducting all-weather vessels with round-the-year plying permission.
- Deploy IPO proceeds with discipline: vessel acquisition only when asset values, charter economics and available vessels meet return thresholds.
- Develop small jetties jointly with coastal industries located away from major ports, deploying own barges, floating cranes and handling equipment for long-duration, relationship-anchored operations.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY2027 expansion priorities set out by the Chairman: scale the coastal cargo movement business built around MV SJ Lily and other coastal vessels (coastal movement commenced during FY2026 through the IFSC subsidiary as well as with the company's own coastal vessels); commission floating-crane lighterage operations at Kolkata and take delivery of two mini bulk carriers on schedule; advance a dry dock yard through its remaining Central-level clearances; progress evaluation of strategic jetty locations in Gujarat and Maharashtra; support the mining joint venture through its clearance milestones towards first coal; and deploy IPO proceeds for vessel acquisition only when asset values, charter economics and available vessels meet return thresholds, with any change to the objects of the Issue subject to shareholder approval. Project and regulatory-clearance risk is managed through staged capital commitment aligned to approval milestones.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- scale: one of the largest midstream lighterage fleets in India — evidence: 63 self-propelled barges, 8 mini bulk carriers, 9 floating cranes, 11 tugs and 1 coastal vessel at FY2026 year-end, plus 370+ earthmoving and shore-handling equipment
- integration: owned sea-to-shore logistics loop from lighterage to shore handling and inland transport — evidence: owned barges, floating cranes and tugs plus 370+ shore-handling units; 16.87 MMT cargo handled and 3.09 MMT cargo transported in FY2026
- distribution: multi-port footprint at Gujarat non-major ports — evidence: three-decade operating presence at Navlakhi, Bedi, Magdalla, Bhavnagar and Dharamtar — against it: the company itself lists dependence on key customers and on Gujarat-coast ports as a concentration risk
- customer lock-in: repeat international government-linked contract — evidence: Ceylon Shipping Corporation coal lightering agreement for the Lakvijaya Power Plant, in place since 2021, extended in June 2026 for two further contract years to 31 May 2028 on unchanged terms
- integration: in-house dry-docking and vessel building to cut fleet downtime — evidence: dry dock yard near Bedi Port with State-level clearances received [planned] — against it: Central-level clearances still in process and the yard is in the name of the Promoter, with ownership presently not transferable for regulatory reasons
- integration: mining-to-movement participation in coal, the largest cargo category — evidence: 37% JV Shreeji Nuravi Chuperbhita Simlong Mines has acquired approximately 1,720 hectares, with coal production targeted from May 2027 [planned] — against it: forest and environment clearance applications are still in final stages of submission

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Cargo-volume and vessel-mix risk — Demand for stevedoring, lighterage and handling services depends on dry-bulk cargo volumes at the ports served (linked to commodity demand, import policies and customer dispatch programmes) and on the mix of geared versus gearless vessels calling there, which drives floating-crane and lighterage demand.
- Monsoon seasonality — Operations at seasonal ports are affected by the monsoon, hitting fleet utilisation; mitigation relies on inducting all-weather mini bulk carriers, with the all-weather count to double to 4 by Q3 FY2027.
- Customer and geographic concentration — Dependence on key customers and on Gujarat-coast ports, with customer and sector concentration inherent in a B2B port-services model; mitigation depends on customer additions and the eastern-India and coastal-movement expansion.
- Project and regulatory-clearance risk — The dry dock yard awaits Central-level clearances and the mining JV's schedule depends on forest, environment and consent approvals; delays would defer the associated revenue streams.
- Fuel and crewing cost inflation — Bunker and diesel price volatility and crewing cost inflation affect operating costs; mitigated through contract structures and operating efficiency.
- Foreign exchange risk — Exposure arises from Sri Lanka operations and USD-denominated receivables.
- Regulatory and compliance risk — The group operates within evolving maritime, tax, labour and environmental frameworks, including the newly notified Labour Codes.
